papers.title: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophile phenotyping by measuring metabolic byproduct formation in microplates
papers.abstract: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophiles can support several low-pH biotechnologies, but their phenotyping remains limited by throughput and inconsistent methods. This study used an assay to monitor metabolic byproduct formation using absorbance indicators in static, oxic cultures in 96-well microplates. In abiotic experiments, ferric iron and/or pH measurements from 51 microplates containing simulant solutions span total iron concentrations of 0-1 M, pH 0.3-7.0, and incubation temperatures of 4-75 {degrees}C. Of these, 30 microplates tested different UV-transparency and gas-permeable membrane configurations. Another 12 microplates tested indicator compatibility with growth media containing ferrous iron and (in)soluble sulfur substrates. Biological experiments measured 438 microplates containing Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans ATCC 23270, Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans ATCC 19377, or Leptospirillum ferriphilum DSM 14647 with chemical additives across 1,400 concentration conditions, yielding 142,038 time-course points, including abiotic controls. Measurements of apparent substrate oxidation and/or growth from 96 culture tubes and 99 shake flasks provide context for microplate observations. The miniaturized assay and this dataset may be useful for microbiology, (critical-mineral) biotechnology development, and synthetic biology.

papers.title: Homologs of the Major Vault Protein defend bacteria against ribotoxins
papers.abstract: Bacteria use sophisticated mechanisms to defend themselves against antibiotics and bacteriophages, yet how they combat toxins deployed during interbacterial competition remains poorly understood. Bacteria use type VI secretion, bacteriocins, and contact dependent inhibition systems to deliver antibacterial toxins that inhibit growth by antagonizing essential processes. Here, we discover that Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses homologs of the eukaryotic major vault protein and a tRNA-like noncoding RNA to defend against RNA-damaging ribotoxins. Using an engineered pyocin delivery system, we showed that P. aeruginosa sensed ribotoxin damage and activated transcription of an RNA repair operon, which included band7, a homolog of the major vault protein. Genetic analyses demonstrated that band7-expressing bacteria were significantly more protected against growth inhibition by a ribotoxin that cleaved the anticodon loop of specific tRNA. Band7 was necessary but not sufficient, and defense also required a non-coding band7 RNA (bRNA). bRNA was cleaved by the ribotoxin, suggesting a mechanism for specificity and defense. Bioinformatic analyses revealed that band7 and candidate bRNA are widely distributed within RNA repair systems across diverse bacteria. Our data suggest that bacteria use structures related to the eukaryotic vault complex to respond to RNA damage thereby providing a hypothesis for the function of the enigmatic human vault.

papers.title: Hyphal differentiation and cell wall remodeling in Trametes versicolor underlie a layered architecture in pure mycelium materials
papers.abstract: Background: Pure mycelium materials grown at the air-liquid interface are promising leather alternatives, yet they are generally treated as homogeneous sheets of fungal biomass. Because basidiomycetes differentiate their hyphae into generative, skeletal and ligative cell types, the properties of such materials may instead arise from an internal tissue organisation. In this study, cell types produced by the trimitic white-rot fungus Trametes versicolor during Liquid State Surface Fermentation were characterized and the impact of their spatial organisation, mechanics and cell wall composition on the resulting material was analysed. Results: Optic and electron microscopy revealed the mats are not homogeneous but consist of two layers: a dense bottom layer of thin-walled generative hyphae in contact with the liquid medium, and a looser, air-exposed top layer made of thick-walled skeletal hyphae. Both layers had comparable hyphal diameters (2.43 {+/-} 0.42 and 2.33 {+/-} 0.50 {micro}m), but the skeletal hyphae in the mat were roughly half the diameter of their fruiting-body counterparts (5.10 {+/-} 1.05 {micro}m). Untreated mats stress-strain curves displayed sequential failure: brittle fracture of the generative bottom layer followed by ductile failure of the skeletal layer. The two faces also differed in wettability, the top being hydrophobic and highly adhesive and the bottom hydrophilic. Solid-state NMR showed extensive rigid cell wall remodelling between the two cell types: alpha-1,3-glucan accounted for about one third of the rigid polysaccharides in the generative layer but was undetectable in the skeletal layer, which contained approximately 74% beta-1,3-glucan and 26% chitin and was overall more rigid and more lipid-rich. Conclusions: These results show that Trametes versicolor differentiates into a very specific type of skeletal hyphae in liquid state surface fermentation, which involves remodelling of the molecular architecture of the cell wall rather than a simple thickening of it, and that the mechanical and surface behaviour of the material can be traced to that remodelling and to the cellular organisation.

papers.title: Emergence of mobile fosA3-blaCTX-M-65 with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) on conjugative plasmids in avian pathogenic Escherichia coli from industrial poultry in Pakistan
papers.abstract: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.

papers.title: Electron Transport Chain-inhibiting fungicides increase resistance to widely used azole antifungals
papers.abstract: Rising antifungal resistance in human and crop fungal pathogens poses significant challenges. Azole-based antifungals that inhibit ergosterol biosynthesis are a key first-line treatment for human fungal infections. Importantly, azole-based ergosterol-inhibiting fungicides are also widely used in agriculture alongside electron transport chain (ETC) Complex III inhibiting compounds. However, it is unknown whether the combined use of these distinct fungicides is entirely synergistic. We find that exposure of fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe to ETC-Complex III inhibitors, prior to or simultaneously with azoles, attenuates azole efficacy by inducing mitochondrial dysfunction. Our analyses show that reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation as a result of ETC inhibition activates oxidative stress response pathways thereby decreasing azole potency. Related responses in pathogenic fungi indicate that the use of ETC inhibiting fungicides in agriculture may inadvertently promote azole resistance. We conclude that the use of specific fungicide combinations should be re-evaluated in order to preserve both their clinical and agricultural effectiveness.

papers.title: Multi-Cohort Blood Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Reproducibility of a 50-Gene Interferon Signature and Benchmarking of a 4-Gene Classifier
papers.abstract: Background: Most blood transcriptomic signatures for tuberculosis (TB) come from a single population or a single platform. Few have been built by meta-analysis and benchmarked against published signatures. Methods: We meta-analysed three UK blood transcriptomic datasets (two Illumina microarray, one RNA-seq; 247 samples: 87 active pulmonary TB (PTB), 160 healthy controls (HC)). GSE107991 reanalyses the Berry test set, and two discovery datasets overlap Sweeney's discovery data, so the datasets are not fully independent. Genes were retained if they replicated in all three studies (FDR 1.5, FDR < 0.01). Performance was estimated in GSE28623 (The Gambia, n = 83) and GSE56153 (Indonesia, n = 36); direction was checked in GSE34608 (Germany, n = 26) and GSE81746 (India, n = 6). A LASSO and random-forest classifier was compared with the Berry 393-gene and Sweeney 3-gene signatures. Immune composition was assessed with MCPcounter and CIBERSORTx. Results: We identified a 50-gene core signature dominated by interferon-stimulated genes. All 50 were upregulated and reached FDR < 0.05 in every dataset. ssGSEA gave an AUC of 0.830 (95% CI 0.743-0.917) in GSE28623 and 0.941 (0.868-1.000) in GSE56153. Direction agreement was 95.7% in Germany and 95.8% in India. PTB versus latent TB infection gave 0.848 (0.756-0.940). LASSO selected four genes (BATF2, ANKRD22, GBP5 and EPSTI1). The frozen classifier gave an external AUC of 0.864 (0.785-0.944). The Sweeney 3-gene score, re-tested in one of its validation cohorts, reached 0.912 and exceeded the 50-gene score (47/50 genes; Holm p = 0.0234). Berry 393-gene scoring gave 0.910 with directions reconstructed from GSE19439 (Holm p = 0.0071 versus the 50-gene score). The signed score is a reconstruction, not Berry's published score. MCPcounter showed myeloid expansion and lymphoid suppression; CIBERSORTx recovered the former but not the broader lymphoid suppression. Conclusions: The 50-gene signature was consistent across three overlapping UK discovery datasets. External evaluation was partial, comprising AUCs for 47 of the 50 genes in two cohorts and direction concordance in two smaller cohorts. This is a benchmarking study, not a claim of superiority: the Sweeney 3-gene and signed Berry scores were higher, and the 4-gene classifier did not differ significantly from Sweeney. The classifier warrants prospective validation. The Berry and Sweeney comparisons are not independent.

papers.title: Environmental heterogeneity and microbial community architecture shape N2O fluxes in intertidal coastal sediments
papers.abstract: Seagrass meadows are key ''blue carbon ecosystems'', yet their contribution to nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions remains poorly constrained. We investigated environmental and microbial descriptors of N2O fluxes in intertidal sediments of Arcachon Bay, home to Europe's largest Zostera noltii meadow. At six sites, we measured in situ N2O fluxes in adjacent bare and vegetated sediments and characterized sediment properties, N2O-cycling genes using qPCR and targeted metagenomics, and microbial co-occurrence networks. Fluxes ranged from -3.7 to 8.4 mol N2O m-2 d-1. Spatial location was the strongest descriptor of flux variation, with inner-bay sites showing higher emissions associated with environmental conditions, carbon accumulation, pH, and microbial community characteristics. Vegetation effects were comparatively small and site-dependent. Metagenomic descriptors of N2O-cycling genes were more informative than qPCR-based descriptors. Taxa associated with nirS (Thiohalophilus), nirK (Planktotalea) and nosZ1 (Roseobacter) were identified as potential contributors to N2O production or reduction, respectively. These findings indicate that spatially structured environmental conditions and microbial community characteristics better describe N2O flux variation than seagrass presence alone. Measurements across tidal and seasonal cycles are needed to establish the temporal consistency of these patterns.

papers.title: Genomic Characterization of a Typical Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli Isolate from an Egyptian Fruit Bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus from Coastal Kenya
papers.abstract: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality cases among young children under the age of five, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

papers.title: Deletion of Furin Facilitates Efficient and Versatile Coronavirus Pseudotyped Particle Generation
papers.abstract: Coronaviruses bring threats to both humans and animals. To initiate successful infections, coronaviruses must first navigate entry into a host cell. Coronavirus spike-bearing pseudotyped particle systems are indispensable tools for studying coronavirus entry and evaluating neutralizing antibodies and entry inhibitors. However, pseudotyped particle titers can be low when packaged particles bear coronavirus spikes that contain the furin cleavage site, and this has been a limitation for pseudotyped particle production and applications. Here, we demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of furin protease in HEK293T cells significantly enhances the production of functional pseudotyped particles bearing spikes containing the furin cleavage site, including those from SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and MHV-JHM. Moreover, deletion of endogenous furin in producer cells yields an effect equivalent to deletion of the furin cleavage site, but with broader application across different spike proteins, and without virus manipulation. This work establishes a simple and effective platform to improve coronavirus pseudotyped particle systems by eliminating furin-mediated pre-activation, enabling more efficient and reliable production for downstream applications.

papers.title: Precision Fermentation Gets a New Player: Genome Assembly and Genetic Transformation of a Novel Strain, Pichia hangzhouana, for Precision Fermentation of Food Ingredients
papers.abstract: Precision fermentation leverages the metabolic pathways of microorganisms to produce valuable proteins and enzymes. Pichia hangzhouana, synonymous with Zygoascus hellenicus, is a non-conventional yeast with potential for food biotechnological applications. This study characterizes the CSIRO strain P. hangzhouana FRR5246, isolated from a tea beverage, to evaluate its suitability as a precision fermentation host for a variety of industrial, agricultural and food production applications. P. hangzhouana demonstrated robust growth across a range of carbon sources, with the highest optical density observed in media containing sucrose or sorbitol as sole carbon source. The yeast showed susceptibility to geneticin, hygromycin B, nourseothricin sulfate, and zeocin sulfate antibiotic agents. Successful genetic transformation was achieved, with the expression of a recombinant orange fluorescent protein (OFP) under the control of the native glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAP1) promoter. The secretome exhibited strong antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, indicating the presence of potent antimicrobial compounds. In addition, whole genome sequencing of P. hangzhouana FRR5246 provided genetic tools for recombinant expression of heterologous genes, insight into the genes, genetic architecture and regulatory mechanisms underlying phenotypic qualities, as well as confirming phylogenetic classification of this strain as clustering with the Dipodascomycetes, most closely related to species Zygoascus hellenicus. P. hangzhouana FRR5246 is a promising candidate for precision fermentation of food ingredients, capable of utilizing diverse carbon sources and producing recombinant proteins. In addition, production of antimicrobial compounds further enhances the potential for biotechnological exploitation. Future work will focus on optimizing growth conditions and exploring native inducible promoters for controlled gene expression.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Environmental Drivers of Maize Microbiome Structure across Diverse Agroecosystems in Georgia, USA
papers.abstract: The understanding of how microbial communities differ across soils, environments, plant tissues, and developmental stages is key to the improvement of crop productivity and resilience. Here, we conducted a statewide survey of maize (Zea mays L.) microbiomes across 35 fields at 16 locations in Georgia, USA, sampling soil, rhizosphere, root interior, and stalk interior at two developmental stages (600 and 1400 growing degree days, GDD). More than 38000 ASVs were produced after amplicon sequencing of 16S rRNA genes. The phyla shown to be dominant are Proteobacteria, Actinobacteriota, Chloroflexi, Planctomycetota, and Acidobacteriota. Based on alpha and beta diversity analyses, the below-ground compartments (soil and rhizosphere) revealed higher diversity and stronger spatial structuring when compared to the above-ground sample types, whereas root and stalk interior microbiomes revealed marked shifts across growth stages. Amino acid metabolism, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, and energy-related pathways predictions (via PICRUSt2) show stage-dependent enrichment. Network analyses show persistent keystone taxa (Proteobacteria and Actinobacteriota) mediating microbial stability, coupled with an increase in modularity and connectivity as we move from early to late growth stages. Some environmental variables, such as temperature, humidity, soil potassium, and soil sodium, showed significant correlation with microbial diversity indicative of a compartment-specific environmental sensitivity. Collectively, our results show that in maize, microbial community composition, interaction, and potential functionality are both impacted by developmental stages and environmental heterogeneity. This study provides a fundamental framework for understanding the microbiome dynamics in field-grown maize across various agroecological conditions. It equally provides ecological insights relevant to microbiome-informed crop management.

papers.title: Comparative landscape of extracellular vesicles across three pathogenic trematodes identifies a key conserved miRNA cargo involved in host liver fibrosis
papers.abstract: Liver fibrosis caused by Schistosoma japonicum, Clonorchis sinensis, and Opisthorchis felineus represents a major global public health burden. Here, we systematically characterized extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by key stages of these parasites and uncovered, for the first time, a conserved repertoire of EV-derived miRNAs shared across all three species. By integrating animal models, single-cell RNA sequencing, and bioinformatic analyses, we comprehensively identified the targetome of miR-36-3p, a cross-species conserved miRNA cargo. Mechanistically, we found that miR-36-3p directly targets Atox1 in Kupffer cells, driving intracellular copper and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and thereby activating hepatic stellate cells. Strikingly, in vivo delivery of an AAV8-encoded miR-36-3p sponge markedly attenuated liver fibrosis across all three infection models. Collectively, these findings establish a conserved, parasite-derived EV miRNA cargo as a previously unrecognized driver of host liver pathology and identify it as a promising therapeutic target for preventing parasite-induced liver fibrosis.

papers.title: A small molecule inhibits Neisseria gonorrhoeae pilus formation
papers.abstract: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is becoming increasingly antimicrobial-resistant. N. gonorrhoeae requires the Type IV pilus (T4p) for pathogenesis, wherein the T4p promotes colonization through adherence to host cells and resistance to neutrophil killing. The pilus also is required for natural transformation and twitching motility. Collectively, these critical functions make the T4p an attractive drug target. Previously, we developed a high-throughput screen to identify compounds with activity against the zinc metalloprotease Mpg, which is involved in T4p biogenesis. Here, we identified a lead compound, SC144, that inhibits Mpg peptidoglycan-hydrolyzing activity in both N. gonorrhoeae and other bacteria encoding Mpg-like M23B metallopeptidase orthologs. Interestingly, SC144 targets Mpgs carboxypeptidase and endopeptidase activities. Importantly, SC144 inhibited N. gonorrhoeae colonization and prevented its survival in two primary human cell culture models of infection without toxic effects on these host cells. This work provides strong evidence that SC144 is a promising lead compound with anti-virulence activity against N. gonorrhoeae.

papers.title: Two novel plant-derived yeast species in Thailandicola (Microbotryomycetes): comparative genomics and transformation
papers.abstract: Plant tissues and surfaces are among the largest microbial habitats on Earth, and commensal yeasts are common members of these communities, where they can contribute to plant-microbe interactions including the biological control of plant diseases. Here, we describe two novel species of unpigmented, basidiomycete yeasts, in the class Microbotryomycetes from the plant phyllosphere (Thailandicola erigeronia and T. cardamina) represented by three isolates from leaves of multiple hosts. We characterize these taxa through analyses of metabolic requirements, tolerance to differences in osmolarity, pH, and temperature, and enzymatic activities. In parallel, we generate near-chromosome-scale hybrid genomes annotated with transcriptome data for these novel species and a congenic isolate. We employ whole-genome and multilocus phylogenetic approaches to infer the placement of these species within a monophyletic clade. We use comparative genomics to examine how the gene content of these yeasts differs from that of other members of the Microbotryomycetes, including an apparent proliferation of retrotransposons. We further demonstrate the genetic transformability of these taxa using Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation. The description of these new species, together with high-quality genome resources and a genetic transformation protocol, establishes a foundation for experimental studies of these novel plant-derived yeasts and their interactions with hosts and other microbes.

papers.title: Detection of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and discrimination of vanA and vanB genotypes by VITEK MS Prime MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry and machine learning
papers.abstract: Rapid identification of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and discrimination of resistance mechanisms (VanA and VanB) are critical for appropriate antimicrobial therapy and infection control, particularly during outbreaks. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), combined with machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool for this purpose. We evaluated whether MALDI-TOF mass spectra acquired on VITEK MS PRIME, combined with machine learning, could provide this information. Spectra from 388 from clinical and rectal surveillance samples (135 vancomycin-susceptible (VSEfm), 138 vanA and 115 vanB VREfm) were processed with Clover MSDAS, and four algorithms (partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), linear and polynomial support vector machines (SVM-L and SVM-P) and random forest (RF)) were trained to discriminate VSEfm from VREfm and VanA from VanB isolates. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation and using independent set of characterized E. faecium isolates from routine practice. Pairwise and triplet ensembles of these algorithms were also assessed. In the test set, PLS-DA was the best individual classifier for VSEfm versus VREfm (balanced accuracy, 78.9%), and the ensemble of PLS-DA and linear SVM reached 80.7%. Validation within routine isolates confirmed the models robustness, achieving 100% correct classification. Discrimination of VanA from VanB was more accurate: 93.2% with RF and up to 97.1% with ensembles. Identical sequence types were found among susceptible, VanA and VanB isolates, indicating that classification was not driven by clonal lineage. MALDI-TOF MS combined with machine learning is a promising, low-cost tool for VREfm screening and vanA/vanB differentiation.

papers.title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
papers.abstract: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

papers.title: Beyond the tripartite genome: a widespread, mobile and gene-rich accessory plasmidome expands the genomic landscape of the model symbiont Sinorhizobium meliloti
papers.abstract: Sinorhizobium meliloti is one of the best-studied nitrogen-fixing symbionts, yet research has focused almost entirely on its chromosome and two megaplasmids, pSymA and pSymB. Many strains carry additional accessory plasmids, but these large, pSymA-like elements are rarely recovered from short-read assemblies, leaving a hidden part of the genome unexplored. By sequencing 346 strains with long reads, we recovered 386 accessory plasmids from 76% of strains, with 318 absent from public databases, showing that accessory plasmids are the rule and not the exception. These plasmids were large (34-749 kb), including the largest accessory plasmid reported in S. meliloti, and most were mobilizable or conjugative (relaxases in 85% and mating-pair formation systems in 75% of plasmid clusters), equipping them to move between strains. RepA typing defined 13 replicon groups unique to Sinorhizobium, which could serve as a framework for tracking these plasmids in natural populations. We also found evidence of plasmid expansion by fusion, and one ~315 kb plasmid was a cointegrate of two smaller plasmids from our collection. About two-thirds of plasmid gene families were absent from the main replicons, including defense systems, the anti-restriction protein ArdC, and biosynthetic gene clusters, 53% of which had never been observed before. Overturning the view that S. meliloti lacks restriction-modification systems, we found them in 153 genomes, including on 32 accessory plasmids. Most inferred gene transfers stayed within the family Rhizobiaceae. Accessory plasmids thus form a large, mobile and largely unexplored gene pool that may shape how this model symbiont competes and adapts.

papers.title: Gene identity, not recoding strategy, determines the fitness cost of synonymous recoding in bacteriophage {Phi}X174
papers.abstract: Synthetic biology allows for the synthesis of genomes from scratch. Although technically achievable, our abilities in designing genomes that result in live organisms are in their infancy. One important consideration is synonymous codon usage bias, which is present in most organisms and shaped by selection for efficient translation. Many studies have edited the synonymous codon usage patterns of viruses with the goal of viral attenuation, but these studies almost always build a single construct per design, so we know little about how repeatable the effects of recoding are. We designed and built 111 synonymously recoded {Phi}X174 genomes, applying four recoding strategies at up to five levels of attenuation to each of three genes, with three independently designed replicates of most combinations. Which gene we recoded mattered considerably more than how we recoded it. Recoding genes for the major capsid protein F, the major spike protein G and the DNA pilot protein H in full, with the least-used synonym codons from E. coli cost 12.0, 10.8 and 5.9 doublings per hour, respectively. Recoding strategy per se had no detectable effect once the number of codons changed was accounted for. Predicted mRNA folding stability also had no measurable effect on fitness when tested in gene F, whose wildtype transcript is highly stable and could easily be destabilized with synonymous codon rearrangements. While the number of codons changed was correlated with the degree of attenuation, divergence between independently designed replicates increased as more codons were edited. Replicates of designs with small fitness effects varied little, while replicates of strongly attenuating designs diverged by several doublings per hour. The fitness outcome of large-scale genome recoding is therefore substantially unpredictable from the design variables alone: even among independently designed genomes receiving the same treatment, fitness can diverge substantially.

papers.title: Pharmacological CARD9 Inhibition Reduces Pneumocystis murina Burden In Vivo and Ex Vivo
papers.abstract: Caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 9 (CARD9) is an important adaptor protein of the innate immune responses to various fungal pathogens, including Pneumocystis species. CARD9 signaling is paramount in Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) host defense, and excessive inflammatory responses driven by this molecule can promote deleterious lung injury. We previously demonstrated that BRD5529, a first generation small-molecule CARD9 inhibitor, attenuates pulmonary inflammatory cytokine production during PCP. Here, we investigated the previously unreported effects of BRD5529 on Pneumocystis murina burden in vivo and in an ex vivo PCP-infected precision-cut lung slice (PCLS) model. In vitro, BRD5529 treatment (1 mg/kg) reduced lung organism burden in mice with established PCP, with an effect similar in magnitude to standard-of-care trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) therapy. In infected PCLS cultured with BRD5529 for 72 h, P. murina viability was also reduced, with the greatest reduction observed at lower BRD5529 concentrations. BRD5529 treatment did not reduce PCLS metabolic activity and viability after 72 h, as assessed by resazurin reduction. Together, these findings suggest that pharmacological CARD9 inhibition may impact organism burden/viability in addition to reducing lung inflammation during PCP.

papers.title: Linking Early Bacterial Responses to Growth Inhibition via Glucose-Turbidity Dynamics for Rapid Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing
papers.abstract: Earlier susceptibility information can guide timely antibiotic selection, while metabolic measurements can broaden the characterization of bacterial drug responses. We developed glucose-turbidity antimicrobial susceptibility testing (GT-AST) to pair residual-glucose assay signals with turbidity and relate early responses to growth inhibition. Among 43 cultured isolates, some antibiotic-exposed cultures showed glucose-associated changes despite attenuated turbidity responses. These observations provide physiological clues for studying metabolic activity when growth is limited, including future investigations of viable but non-culturable states or persister cells. Conventional broth microdilution relies on overnight growth readings; GT-AST used trajectories collected during approximately 2 h of antibiotic exposure to predict subsequent growth and estimate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs). Across 100 repeats of isolate-grouped cross-validation, essential agreement between predicted MICs and independently measured reference MICs averaged 87.1%. Eight bronchoalveolar lavage fluid specimens were tested directly without prior bacterial isolation. Levofloxacin susceptibility classifications based on observed growth agreed with hospital results in all four culture-positive specimens. Exact and essential agreement between predicted and hospital MICs each averaged 99.0%. Together, these findings support developing GT-AST to provide earlier susceptibility information for effective, appropriately targeted treatment of patients. Keywords: antimicrobial susceptibility testing; glucose metabolism; turbidity; machine learning; minimum inhibitory concentration

papers.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Host Gene Expression Patterns Associated with Naegleria fowleri Infection in the Murine Brain
papers.abstract: Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM), caused by the free-living amoebae Naegleria fowleri, is a devastating disease with a mortality rate exceeding 97%. Despite its severity, the spatial and temporal characteristics of the host immune response to infection within the brain remain poorly understood. Here, we used spatially resolved transcriptomic profiling to characterize region-specific gene expression patterns in brain tissue collected at multiple time points following intranasal inoculation of N. fowleri in mice. Our analysis revealed pronounced pro-inflammatory transcriptional signatures that varied across brain regions and over the course of infection. Cell type-associated gene expression profiles suggested the involvement of several immune cell populations, including macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer T cells, alongside transcriptional changes associated with neural cell populations. Notably, inflammatory transcriptional signatures also were detected in brain regions without detectable amoebae, indicating that host responses extend beyond regions of apparent parasite localization. Collectively, these findings provide a spatial and temporal characterization of the host transcriptional response during experimental PAM, highlighting inflammatory gene expression signatures and putative immune and neural cell populations associated with disease progression. This study provides a foundation for future investigations into the cellular and molecular processes underlying neuroinflammation during N. fowleri infection.

papers.title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia
papers.abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.

papers.title: MetaEntropy: quantifying protein variability in complex viral mixtures via entropy
papers.abstract: High-density sequence data has become commonplace in the study of complex viral mixtures from wastewater. Established algorithms are available for lineage deconvolution and labelling of clinically-elusive mutations. However, less attention has been paid to the quantification of translated amino acid diversity. We present MetaEntropy, a modular R package for assessing protein sequence variability and identifying sites under potential selection via Shannon entropy. MetaEntropy integrates utility functions for visualizing genome-wide and protein-specific variability, extracting nucleotide and amino acid mutation profiles, and identifying entropy hotspots. Despite being designed for wastewater surveillance, the package can also profile protein diversity from cross-sectional intra-patient data. However, it does not analyze population structure or quasispecies, for which several tools are available. By focusing on positional entropy, MetaEntropy bypasses the sequence constraints, computational overhead, and consensus-based variant loss typical of traditional haplotype reconstruction and multiple sequence alignment strategies. To balance sensitivity against neutral variation, the package evaluates entropy using a standard 20-class canonical amino acid scheme and a 7-class model based on traditional physicochemical properties. Calculated entropy values are normalized to a 0-1 scale, enabling direct comparisons of protein diversity across loci and sample strata. As proofs of concept, we employ MetaEntropy to detect well-known SARS-CoV-2 functional changes from wastewater data, and to explore tissue-specific heterogeneity in systemic infections. MetaEntropy is available from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) at https://CRAN.R-project.org/.

papers.title: Charge-engineered nanohybrid coatings for microbial fouling resistance
papers.abstract: Microbial attachment is the gateway to biofouling and microbially influenced corrosion. Yet biocides and passive barrier coatings do not actively regulate the charged metal-microbe interface at which adhesion begins. Here we report a charge-engineered coating, a graphene thin-film nanohybrid (gTFN) on nickel (Ni) forming an asymmetric metal-graphene-metal junction, that suppresses cell attachment through interfacial charge redistribution rather than soluble toxicity. Against the model sulfate-reducing bacterium Oleidesulfovibrio alaskensis G20, gTFN combines an impermeable graphene scaffold, an immobilized low-leaching Ag cap and a serrated topology, reducing microbial surface coverage by 98%, increasing charge-transfer resistance 47-fold and lowering corrosion current 167-fold relative to Ni. Surface-potential mapping and density functional theory reveal interfacial dipoles that pattern the surface potential, while imaging shows graphene wrinkles channeling residual attachment. Transcriptomic profiling reveals downregulation of biofilm-associated and energy-metabolism genes. These results establish interfacial charge redistribution as an active antifouling and anticorrosion mechanism for controlling microbial biointerfaces.

papers.title: HIV-1 Mutational Bias Shapes the Supply of Drug Resistance Mutations
papers.abstract: The development of durable HIV-1 therapeutics requires understanding not only which mutations confer resistance, but also how readily those mutations arise. Prior work has characterized the effects of individual mutations on viral fitness and drug or immune escape; however, the contribution of mutational bias to HIV-1 evolutionary pathways remains largely unquantified. Here, we report and provide an interactive HIV-1 Mutation Rate Atlas (MRA), built on a dataset of empirical measurements of single-cycle HIV-1 mutation accumulation in the absence of selection pressure, using error-corrected long-read sequencing. The MRA estimates the mutation rate at every genomic position to each possible nucleotide, enabling evaluation of amino acid mutability across the genome. Using the MRA, we show that mutation rate biases predict HIV-1 drug resistance variant frequencies across patients. These results demonstrate that mutational biases shape HIV-1 evolutionary outcomes, providing a framework for predicting HIV-1 evolution and drug resistance.

papers.title: Pyrenophora teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures to facilitate effector-driven promotion of in planta colonization on barley
papers.abstract: Pyrenophora teres f. teres is a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that causes net form net blotch (NFNB) of barley. Infection of susceptible barley leaves initially causes dot-like lesions that progress to transverse and longitudinal striations, that form the net-like pattern of necrosis for which the disease was named. While the complex genetic architecture of the P. teres f. teres-barley interaction involves both dominant resistance and susceptibility and quantitative resistance, the in planta infection structures, compatible infection timeline, and the influence of effectors remain poorly defined. This study used fluorescent staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to define infection structures and characterize the compatible infection timeline of P. teres f. teres. Using CLSM in conjunction with image-segmentation machine learning, we generated a clear comparative infection timeline showing how P. teres f. teres isolates harboring zero, one, or two virulence effector alleles infect the barley cultivar Rika. We believe that the effector genes VR1 and VR2 contributed to virulence in a synergistic manner. The effector genes combined presence accelerated the timing and spread of programmed cell death, resulting in significantly greater hyphal volume and visibly more severe macroscopic lesion development. This suggests that P. teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures alongside effectors to maximize fungal colonization and hyphal positioning to optimize nutrient uptake, perpetuating its polycyclic life cycle.

papers.title: Multiple Glycans and IFITM Proteins Mediate Human Coronavirus OC43 entry
papers.abstract: Human coronavirus (HCoV)-OC43 is the most prevalent seasonal coronavirus, causing colds, and occasional severe disease. HCoV-OC43 attachment is reportedly mediated by 9-O acetylated sialic acid (9-O-Ac-Sia); no proteinaceous receptor has been identified. Using genome-wide CRISPR-cas9 screens, we identify several host factors that mediate HCoV-OC43 entry. First, we identify NXPE3, an esterase, as required for HCoV-OC43 attachment and infection, both in vitro and in vivo, and demonstrate a previously unknown role for NXPE3 in 9-O-Ac-Sia synthesis. However, we further show that single residue substitutions in HCoV-OC43 spike, in the S1A domain at the 9-O-Ac-Sia binding site, or two substitutions in the S1B domain, confer 9-O-Ac-Sia independence and a switch to heparan sulfate-dependent entry. Additionally, we find that IFITM1/2/3 proteins act post-attachment to drive HCoV-OC43 virion-cell fusion and entry, irrespective of which attachment mechanism is used. Thus, flexible use of glycan attachment factors enables HCoV-OC43 to access fusion-driving IFITM proteins during entry.

papers.title: Deletion of two candidate depolymerases with overlapping genetic effects increases PHA yield in Rhodopseudomonas palustris TIE-1
papers.abstract: Polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) is a microbial carbon-storage polymer with potential as a renewable bioplastic, but intracellular remobilization can limit polymer retention. The metabolically versatile bacterium Rhodopseudomonas palustris TIE-1 accumulates PHA during photoheterotrophic growth, yet the enzymes that control PHA turnover in this organism remain incompletely studied. We identified PhaZ2 (Rpal_0568) as a second candidate PHA depolymerase that is evolutionarily and architecturally distinct from the previously annotated PhaZ1 (Rpal_0578). Deleting either PhaZ1 or PhaZ2 alone did not substantially increase PHA content under tested growth conditions, whereas the double mutant accumulated 2.3-fold and 1.7-fold more PHA than wild type under non-nitrogen-fixing and nitrogen-fixing photoheterotrophic conditions, respectively, supporting overlapping roles in PHA turnover. All deletion strains showed longer doubling times but reached final culture densities similar to wild type. The double mutant showed its strongest retention phenotype under severe but growth-permissive nutrient limitation, including 3.7-fold more PHA than wild type at 33% phosphorus availability. A two-stage cultivation strategy that separated biomass formation from nutrient-limited storage raised volumetric PHA titer to 0.180 mg per mL culture in the double mutant, 1.5-fold more than wild type and approximately 3.4-fold higher than single-stage 33% phosphorus limitation and 4.0-fold higher than single-stage 8% nitrogen limitation (cross-experiment comparison), despite lower PHA content per unit biomass. Finally, an LC-MS-calibrated FTIR spectroscopy model predicted PHA content with an R2 of 0.928 (n = 15) and reproduced the major biological trends. These results identify genetically redundant candidate depolymerases as targets for improving PHA retention in TIE-1 and establish a cultivation and screening framework for strain engineering. Importance Persistent pollution from petroleum-based plastics has intensified the need for biodegradable plastics produced from renewable resources. Polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) is a microbially synthesized bioplastic, but microbial cells can also consume the stored polymer, reducing its net yield. The metabolically versatile, photosynthetic purple non-sulfur bacterium (PNSB) Rhodopseudomonas palustris TIE-1 is a promising production organism because it can photosynthesize, assimilate atmospheric nitrogen, and utilize diverse carbon sources. We show that two candidate PHA depolymerases, PhaZ1 and PhaZ2, likely have overlapping roles in PHA turnover. Removing both candidates increased polymer retention, particularly when nitrogen or phosphorus was limited, and a two-stage cultivation strategy further increased PHA titer to 0.180 mg per mL of culture. We also developed a rapid infrared spectroscopy method to track polymer content across strains and growth conditions. These findings offer complementary genetic, cultivation, and screening strategies for improving microbial bioplastic production and may help advance sustainable alternatives to petroleum-derived plastics.

papers.title: Targeting host eIF4A with zotatifin inhibits Bundibugyo virus and other filoviruses
papers.abstract: Filoviruses, including Ebola and Marburg viruses, depend on host eIF4A helicase activity for replication. Zotatifin is a first in class, clinical stage eIF4A inhibitor that acts as a molecular glue, stabilizing the interaction between eIF4A and selected polypurine rich RNA sequences, thereby inhibiting RNA unwinding and ribosomal scanning. Here, we identify pronounced polypurine enrichment in the 5'untranslated regions (5'UTRs) of the seven major filoviral protein-coding genes NP, VP35, VP40, GP, VP30, VP24, and L across four virus species, including Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). Consistent with these findings, zotatifin inhibits the replication of Ebola, Marburg, Sudan, Tai Forest, and Bundibugyo viruses at low nanomolar concentrations. Zotatifin has been administered to humans in oncology and COVID19 clinical studies. Clinical pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling indicates that exposures resulting in inhibition of BDBV replication are achievable in humans at tolerated doses following subcutaneous administration. Together, these findings support the repurposing of zotatifin as a host directed antiviral candidate against BDBV and other filoviruses, with potential applications in preparedness for future outbreaks.

papers.title: The virome of New Zealand fur seals reveals novel viral diversity and evidence of continued Canine distemper virus circulation
papers.abstract: Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaik[o]ura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaik[o]ura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaik[o]ura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.
